projects.name: Mau5head v2
projects.summary: This year's rebuild of my deadmau5 helmet. The shell is clear PETG with LEDs glued into printed slots, 622 of them across the face and ears, so the whole head becomes a screen.

facts.Shell: Clear PETG, printed on a Prusa XL
facts.Lights: 622 WS2815: 398 in the shell (the print has slots for 948), 224 in the ears
facts.Controller: GLEDOPTO Elite running WLED, driven from a phone
facts.CAD: Parametric CadQuery model, edited in Onshape

details: Pixel pockets stop 0.8 mm short of the outer surface, so the shell diffuses each LED into a square dot
The visor hinges up on pivots hidden inside the shell, with a perforated mesh panel to see through
Ears are two-part prints lit by LED strips inside polycarbonate tubes, like a lightsaber blade
Shows are pre-programmed to songs and run from a phone on the helmet's own Wi-Fi, with no laptop and no router
projects.writeup:
The shell was the easy half. This is the software: a 622-LED helmet that has to know where every LED physically is, has to stay cool enough to wear, and has to run a show off a phone with no laptop and no Wi-Fi in the room.

Finding the LEDs

The print has a slot for every shell LED, 948 of them, plus three tubes and a rim channel in each ear. What it can't tell you is which LED went where. All 622 hang off one data wire, and an LED's number is only how far along that wire it sits. The CAD lists the order the strips were meant to be wired in. The map has to find out what was actually built.

I started by hand: light each strip in turn and write down where it starts and stops. Then by camera: each LED lit alone in a dark room, photographed, and the centre of its glow recorded, 622 times. Two things went wrong along the way. A reference LED, re-measured every so often to catch the camera being nudged, kept appearing to jump 200 pixels. It hadn't moved. Its centroid was sometimes landing on a reflection, so three references and a similarity fit replaced it. And a camera fitted to the shell came out perfect, 0.000 px, after the worst-fitting points were dropped twice. The survivors had walked onto one patch of the sphere, and a flat set of points fits a camera exactly while saying nothing about depth. There's a guard against that now.

The map that graded itself

The CAD's wiring order and the camera disagreed by about 15 pixels, so my first map slid each LED along the sphere until it sat on its own camera ray. It then matched that camera to 0.02 px. That should have been the giveaway: a map built from a camera will always agree with it.

From the front, the one direction it was built from, it looked right. From the side it was wrong. A front camera barely constrains anything near the edge of a sphere, so LEDs there had drifted as far as 113 mm, most of the shell sat between slots where no LED can be, and every ear LED had the same depth: one flat sheet. I only saw it by turning the simulator side-on.

Slots, not coordinates

The fix was to stop letting the camera place anything. Every position now comes from the CAD, and the cameras only decide which slot each LED is in.

That needed a second view. I moved the camera up and to the right, about 34° from the first, and measured all 622 again. Two views fix a point instead of a ray, and with nothing assumed about the helmet, the shell LEDs triangulate to a median of 173.3 mm from the centre of the head. The CAD's LED sphere is 173.0 mm, so the cameras could be trusted.

The chain is then lined up against the CAD's wiring order with dynamic programming. Each LED is the next slot along its strip, or skips an empty slot, or starts the next strip at either end, and no slot can be used twice. A camera that sees an LED edge-on counts for less than one that sees it square-on, because a glow at a grazing angle is clipped by its own recess and its centre shifts by 30 to 40 px. Both cameras are re-solved against the slots they picked, and it goes round again.

It converges starting from nothing but the CAD. 398 shell LEDs land in 398 different slots, with exactly one slot empty, at the top of strip B04. The strips beside the ear mounts turn out to be wired in a different order from the CAD's list, in the same mirror-image pattern on both sides. Run each camera through the whole thing alone, with no help from the other, and both pick the same slot for all 398. Where a camera sees an LED square-on the error is 2 px. The original mapping was off by 15.

The walk had it first

Then I compared the result with the hand walk from the first night. The cameras found 68 strips and so did the walk, and 67 of the boundaries are in exactly the same place. The odd one out is a single LED among the two-LED strips at the chin. The walk had recorded all three surprises by eye: the shell ends at LED 397, one strip has 11 LEDs instead of 12, and the strips at the mounts run out of order. The original map had overridden every one of them with the CAD's numbers.

The ears

The ears are where the cameras are weakest. They're only calibrated on the shell, the ear glows are wide and diffuse, and when I fitted each ear's position to its own LEDs, it matched a daylight photo worse than the CAD's position did. Drawn through the high camera, the CAD outline lands on the real ears in that photo. So the ears stay exactly where the CAD puts them, tilted back and turned outward, and the cameras only decide where along which tube each LED sits: up and back along three tubes, then around the rim. A camera measures that part well, whatever the depth.

Effects as geometry, not as a grid

The helmet is not a screen. It is a patch of sphere with a visor slot cut out of it and two discs on the sides, and the strips that survive are all different lengths. So an effect is written against where an LED is — its height, its angle around the face, its position on its own ear — and never against a row and column that do not exist. Thirty-seven of them, from a plain colour wash to a spectrum analyser.

Text is the awkward case. Letters are rasterised into a small bitmap and then sampled by each LED's own position, because blitting to a grid would bend the letterforms around the sphere. On this dome 27% of the cells contain no LED at all, so a quarter of every glyph used to vanish silently; every lit cell that catches no LED now claims the nearest one.

Keeping it wearable

622 WS2815s at full white is about 11.8 A. The helmet is on somebody's head, glued together, with no airflow. The limit that matters is not current but heat, so the power model is a leaky bucket over delivered energy: peaks are allowed, and sustained output is rationed back towards what the helmet can actually shed. The rule is that nothing stays raised for ten minutes or more, and that is a test rather than a comment — it asserts the draw after ten minutes of worst-case content, plus the invariant that delivered energy can never exceed what the helmet sheds in that time plus one bucketful.

Sizing that bucket is where intuition fails. The obvious number was exactly ten minutes' worth of excess watts, and it broke the rule: full-bright content starts near 25 W and the allowance eases down rather than stepping, so at ten minutes it was still drawing 14.3 W. The number had to be measured, not derived.

Making the shows follow the music

A show is a cue list built from an analysis of the track — beats, bars, sections, per-band energy — with effects quantised to the beat grid so they land on the bar instead of drifting past it.

Whether that is working is not something you can judge by watching thirty seconds. Scoring it over the whole track found the helmet's brightness correlating +0.02 with the music on one song: the loud effects had landed in the quiet sections and it was running beside the track rather than with it. The cause was the thermal budget holding every show flat at its sustained floor for its entire length. Re-sizing it took the average correlation from +0.23 to +0.43.

The controller has no room to store songs, so starting a show used to light the helmet in silence. Now the first time a show starts, the page asks for the track and keeps it in the phone's browser storage. After that, starting the show plays the song, and the lights follow its clock through pauses and seeks.

No laptop, no network

At a show there is no Wi-Fi worth trusting. The helmet brings up its own access point and serves the controller page off the LED controller's own filesystem — 76 kB, any phone, nothing installed. That location is forced rather than chosen: a browser cannot send UDP, an https page cannot reach a plain-http address on the local network, and a plain-http page is not a secure context, so it cannot be cached by a service worker or served from a laptop that is not there.

Which meant porting the whole engine, the power guard and the show player to JavaScript. They are ports, and the test suite keeps them honest: every effect is rendered in both languages at seven times each and compared, and they agree to 0.0003 of a count out of 255.

Running it against the real controller found four things that all failed the same way — by sending successfully and changing nothing. Writing pixels blanks the rest of the strip, so deltas were showing a fifth of each frame. A WebSocket message that spans two TCP packets is dropped in silence. The firmware never acknowledges a pixel write, so pacing on acknowledgements pinned it at 4 fps. And the brightness limiter was being set on a key the firmware accepts and ignores. None of that is visible without reading the strip back, so there is a tool that does.

The two videos

The first video above is all of this in ninety seconds: the slots, the walk, the self-grading map seen from the side, the second camera, the alignment filling in the shell strip by strip, the ears inside their tubes, and the old map against the new from every side. The footage is from the first night; everything else is drawn from the data. The second video is the original localisation pass replayed, each centroid plotted as it was measured, in wiring order, so the faint line between the dots is the wire.

The last six photos are the other passes. A flat bar swept down the helmet, which is the sharpest test of a position map because it is differential — it asks whether a set of LEDs lit at the same moment, and diffusion cannot blur that away. The supply ramped in steps until something gave, to find where the wiring actually stops being stable rather than where the nameplate says. And the colour-order hunt, which is a yes-or-no question — light a span red, photograph it, see whether green comes back — so the search can halve.

One thing those pictures gave away by accident. The diagonal banding across the ears in the supply-ramp shot is not an effect: it is the LED tubes showing through the diffuser. It had been reported as “a line on the ears” and assumed to be a mapping fault for a week. Every LED on the ear is lit in that photograph, so the pattern is purely where they physically are, and no amount of software evens it out.

Try it

The simulator runs the same engine, power guard and show player as the helmet, on this map, drawn inside the helmet's own CAD. Play your own song and the effects follow it; pick one of my shows and it plays to your copy of its song. The audio never leaves the page. The source is on GitHub, and the map is built by mau5slots.py.

projects.name: SAO MANY SAOs
projects.summary: A DEF CON 33 badge that powers and displays 25 SAOs at once. I designed it, had it made, tested every board, and sold it at DEF CON and through Hacker Warehouse.

facts.Power: 2 × 18650, charged over USB or barrel jack
facts.Lights: White ARGB edge LEDs, driven by the SmartAO

details: Every SAO port has a notch on the left for tying on a leash
Red and green LEDs next to the batteries show charging and full
If the badge is on while charging, the power goes to the SAOs instead of the cells
The kit included printed clips that add a leash ring to keyhole-style SAOs
SmartAO: a companion hex SAO with an RP2040, USB-C, and BOOT/RST buttons. It plugs into the top-left slot and runs the edge LED animations
projects.writeup:
I built SAO MANY SAOs because I had a simple problem: I'd collected a bunch of SAOs, and there was no good way to power and display them all at once. Most badges support one or two. I wanted something that could handle all of them at the same time without being fragile or just decorative.

Learning PCB design

When I started, I didn't know how to design a production-ready PCB at this scale. I learned by doing: watching tutorials, asking questions in Discord servers, and iterating quickly. A lot of the early work was figuring out how to route power safely across a large board and keep signals clean with that many connectors.

The layout was the hardest part. Supporting 25 SAOs meant thinking carefully about spacing, mechanical stress, and how people would plug things in without snapping headers. SAOs vary a lot in current draw, so the power design had to handle the worst case without failing.

Once I had a working design, I ordered prototypes and tested them with real SAOs, mixing high-draw and low-draw modules, checking voltage stability, and making sure everything behaved. I revised the design from that testing before the production run.

Production

I handled most of the assembly myself, with help soldering and prepping units. Every board was tested for power, charging, and SAO connections before it shipped. I was involved in every step, from PCB design to packaging, pricing, and getting badges into people's hands at DEF CON.

How it went

I shared it on Reddit and in the badgelife community. The response was really positive, especially from people who already owned lots of SAOs and never had a way to show them all at once. It pushed me to learn PCB design, power management, manufacturing constraints, and how to ship a real hardware product to real users.

projects.name: Mau5head v1
projects.summary: My first deadmau5 helmet: a 3D-printed head with sound-reactive WLED strips around the ears and mouth. Someone bought it for about $700.

facts.Parts: Six major pieces plus the mesh, joined with dovetails
facts.Finish: Primer, black, graphite powder, 2K clear coat

projects.writeup:
Lights

The lights run on a WLED controller I bought on Amazon for $30, with addressable RGB strips soldered to it. It's sound reactive because it has a small microphone, which works great as a wall display, but I couldn't get it to work well while walking around.

To power it I carried a 300 W Anker backup battery. I could have used something smaller, but I already owned it and didn't want to spend more. The controller and LEDs run at 12 V, so I used the battery's wall plug.

Printing

I printed it on a Prusa XL and my Bambu P1P, split into six major pieces plus the mesh. Dovetails made the joints easier, and I melted them together with a soldering iron and a little glue. The ears are lightweight PLA, attached with epoxy and two large bolts I had lying around.

Paint

After some sanding I used about one can of Duplicolor automotive primer, then black spray paint. On top of that I rubbed in graphite powder to make it silvery, which shows in the photos with more light, and locked it in with 2K clear coat.

Assembly

I got a hard hat for free from my neighborhood Facebook group, cut out the brim and sides with a Dremel, and cut two large rectangles so it could pass through the ear slots. I glued it in with two-part epoxy and epoxy putty, plus a lot of clamps and duct tape.

I sold it for roughly $700, which is why there's a version 2.

details: Notes come from carriage speed: frequency ÷ steps per mm
Microstepping drops from 16× to 4× during playback for more volume
Percussion is a short, fast Z move; direction alternates so Z doesn't drift
Separate 10-second tuning files for each note, checked with a phone tuner
